editorial_policy.summary: Historical stories are static and reviewed. Private mental states are never inferred. Critical interpretations are optional and labeled.
editorial_policy.coverage_note: This draft contains one deliberately small connected cluster to demonstrate a platform designed for any artist universe. Coverage is not a complete biography or discography.

universes.name: Tyler, the Creator
universes.tagline: Albums as chapters in a changing creative language.
universes.summary: A reviewed demo path through Tyler's early collective context and the creative contrast critics identified between Cherry Bomb and Flower Boy.

albums.title: Bastard
albums.summary: The opening chapter establishes Tyler's early fictional therapy framing, home-produced sound, and confrontational writing.
albums.before: Created before Odd Future reached a large audience, this self-released project introduces ideas and characters that continue into the next releases. The archive treats the fictional narration separately from Tyler's real private psychology.

albums.title: Goblin
albums.summary: A larger-stage continuation of the early fictional world, arriving as Odd Future's visibility rapidly expanded.
albums.before: Odd Future's 2011 interviews capture a group suddenly encountering television performances, established artists, and intense attention while Tyler prepared Goblin.

albums.title: Wolf
albums.summary: A more melodic and arranged chapter that keeps the fictional camp setting while allowing more autobiography and reflection into the writing.
albums.before: By 2013, Odd Future was no longer only an online discovery. Its members were developing distinct solo careers, and Tyler's production palette was becoming a larger part of the story.

albums.title: Cherry Bomb
albums.summary: A dense, abrasive and highly arranged chapter that critics later used as a contrast point for Flower Boy.
albums.before: The reviewed draft does not claim a single event caused this album or the one after it. It treats the documented music and later criticism as separate evidence.

albums.title: Flower Boy
albums.summary: A chapter widely described by critics as more reflective, concise, and open than Tyler's earlier work.
albums.before: Contemporary criticism placed the album after years of provocative public work and emphasized a turn toward reflection. This is a critical framing, not a diagnosis of Tyler's private state.

albums.title: IGOR
albums.summary: A tightly sequenced character-driven album that follows attraction, jealousy, loss, and attempted acceptance across a relationship triangle.
albums.before: After Flower Boy's critical reception, Tyler built an album around a distinct visual persona and a continuous emotional sequence rather than separating rap and production into different lanes.

albums.title: CALL ME IF YOU GET LOST
albums.summary: A travel-stamped rap album hosted by DJ Drama, balancing public confidence and luxury with a private romantic conflict.
albums.before: Following IGOR's continuous relationship narrative, Tyler returned to a mixtape-host format while retaining the detailed world-building and sequencing of his album work.

albums.title: CHROMAKOPIA
albums.summary: A masked, highly personal chapter organized around adulthood, privacy, family lessons, public attention, and responsibility.
albums.before: Released three years after CALL ME IF YOU GET LOST, this chapter arrived with the St. Chroma visual identity and placed questions of visibility and adult responsibility at the center of the album world.

albums.title: DON'T TAP THE GLASS
albums.summary: A short, movement-focused record that shifts from CHROMAKOPIA's guarded reflection toward physical energy and dance-floor immediacy.
albums.before: Released nine months after CHROMAKOPIA and during a world-tour period, the album was presented as a concise 10-song project built around movement rather than a dense explanatory concept.

chapters.title: From density to reflection
chapters.dek: Critics heard Flower Boy as a more focused and introspective chapter, while tracing parts of its musical vocabulary back through Cherry Bomb.

universes.name: Odd Future
universes.tagline: A collective whose shared world opened into many solo universes.
universes.summary: A reviewed overview of an internet-native Los Angeles collective and the distinct creative paths connected to it.
universes.coverage: Core collective catalog: 2008–2012; reviewed story coverage: 2008–2018

albums.title: The Odd Future Tape
albums.summary: The collective's first mixtape documents the original combinations of Tyler, Hodgy, Casey Veggies, Jasper, and other early participants.
albums.before: Released before Odd Future's wider internet-era breakthrough, the tape is cataloged here as an early group document. Track credits follow the MusicBrainz release record, while unavailable official videos remain search-only.

albums.title: Radical
albums.summary: A full-collective mixtape built from short solo turns, pairings, and posse tracks across the expanding Odd Future roster.
albums.before: Radical arrived during the period when the collective was distributing its own work online. The archive separates the documented track list from later claims about the group's cultural impact.

albums.title: 12 Odd Future Songs
albums.summary: A label-era compilation that gathers tracks by Tyler, MellowHype, Mike G, Domo Genesis, The Jet Age of Tomorrow, and The Internet.
albums.before: This compilation is not a single newly recorded group statement; it is included because it offers a concise map of the connected artists and subgroups active around Odd Future in 2011.

albums.title: The OF Tape Vol. 2
albums.summary: Odd Future's studio album moves between member spotlights and ensemble records, ending with the extended group showcase Oldie.
albums.before: By 2012, members and subgroups had distinct catalogs of their own. The album presents those voices side by side instead of treating Odd Future as one uniform performer.

documents.title: Odd Future's internet-native world
documents.text: Odd Future used Tumblr and YouTube to publish music alongside informal photos and videos of the collective working, skating, eating, and spending time together. Pitchfork's retrospective argues that this access helped the group grow from local friends into a community with a highly engaged audience.

documents.title: Distinct creative identities inside the collective
documents.text: A Pitchfork retrospective describes Odd Future as a shared platform for members with notably different creative identities, including Tyler, the Creator, Frank Ocean, Earl Sweatshirt, Syd, Domo Genesis, and the production groups surrounding them.

documents.title: Odd Future speaking as a group in 2011
documents.text: A March 2011 interview at SXSW captured Tyler, Hodgy, Syd, Domo Genesis, Left Brain, and Mike G discussing their sudden visibility, Tyler's upcoming Goblin album, live appearances, and encounters with established artists.

documents.title: Critics describe a creative shift on Flower Boy
documents.text: Contemporary reviews characterized Flower Boy as more meditative, concise, and introspective than Tyler's earlier releases. That language belongs to critics; it should not be presented as a clinical statement or as proof of Tyler's private psychological state.

documents.title: A critical reading of Where This Flower Blooms
documents.text: The New Yorker's 2017 listening note reads Where This Flower Blooms as a reflection on adulthood, self-definition, isolation, and growth. It identifies Frank Ocean's backing vocals and treats the song's message to young Black listeners as part of that reading.

documents.title: What this draft can verify about Pharrell's influence
documents.text: The reviewed retrospective connects Tyler's message of creative self-definition to the importance he placed on Pharrell's work. This draft does not contain a primary source proving that one private studio intervention directly caused Flower Boy or Where This Flower Blooms, so it does not state that causal story as fact.

documents.title: Syd's public account of learning production
documents.text: In a 2015 TIME interview, Syd said she built a studio in her parents' guesthouse as a teenager and originally wanted to be a producer who also sang hooks. She named Pharrell as a model for that ambition.

documents.title: The Internet's home-studio collaboration
documents.text: Syd and Matt Martians told TIME that they met online, later became roommates, and worked in a living-room studio. Their account describes an everyday collaborative environment rather than a single dramatic origin event.

documents.title: Syd's public context for Penthouse Cloud
documents.text: TIME reported that Syd wrote Penthouse Cloud the morning after the decision in the Michael Brown case. Syd and Matt Martians described the song as philosophical rather than a conventional political protest song.
